item.text: {"question_id":"3B.5","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi’s state of siege in North Kivu and Ituri remained an expansive, rights-restrictive emergency regime originally imposed in May 2021. By May 2023, Amnesty reported that it had been extended more than 50 times over the preceding two years, without meaningful public debate on the legality or merits of the extensions; civilian administration had been transferred to military and police authorities, civilian courts replaced by military courts for prosecuting civilians, and the authorities had not met the reported international notification requirement for derogations (BATCH-0012-R03-E001; BATCH-0012-R03-E003; BATCH-0012-R03-E007). Amnesty also reported systematic rights restrictions, harassment and imprisonment of journalists, mass pretrial detention, and serious security-force abuses by authorities appointed by Tshisekedi, while attacks on civilians and displacement worsened over the 2021–2023 period; these outcomes do not by themselves establish that Tshisekedi personally ordered every abuse (BATCH-0009-E002; BATCH-0012-R03-E004). Direct 2023 application of the coercive security environment is illustrated by the 18 January Goma protest, when police used tear gas against an unauthorized demonstration and authorities detained some protesters and journalists; the source does not establish a personal presidential order, legal grounds, scale of detention, or remedy (BATCH-0008-E008). There was contrary evidence of review and a possible corrective shift: Tshisekedi convened an August 2023 roundtable with state, community, religious, civil-society, and citizen representatives to consider maintaining, requalifying, or lifting the regime, acknowledged that it should not last indefinitely, and in October announced gradual easing, including ending a curfew and allowing peaceful demonstrations. The supplied record does not show the roundtable’s recommendations, full implementation of the easing by year-end, or repeal of the state of siege (BATCH-0007-E002; BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0008-E007). The 2023 press-law revision also retained possible imprisonment for press offenses, and Bujakera was arrested and held in pretrial detention under false-information, forgery, press, and penal provisions, although the evidence does not establish Tshisekedi’s personal direction of that case (BATCH-0025-E007; BATCH-0025-E012). Overall, the evidence supports broad and insufficiently constrained emergency administration with partial review and an unverified late-year easing, rather than demonstrated narrow, lawful, consistently remedied use of exceptional
